What is the CREV per-task ritual?
column2: Context (switch to right cluster) → Read (parse the task, note namespace) → Execute (do it, imperative first) → Verify (confirm with get/describe). Do it every single task.

column1: What three golden shell shortcuts should you set up first in the exam?
column2: alias k=kubectl, export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml" (the "do" generator), and export now="--force --grace-period=0" (delete now).

column1: How do you switch kubectl context to a named cluster in the exam?
column2: kubectl config use-context <name>. Always the FIRST action of every task (the C in CREV).

column1: What is the TRSVR drill loop?
column2: Task → Read → Solve → Verify → Reset. The repeatable practice cycle for each drill.

column1: What is the LEDGE debug order for a failing app?
column2:
Logs → Events → Describe → Get (wide) → Exec. Work outside-in, cheapest signal first.
kubectl logs <pod>                 # app said what?
kubectl logs <pod> --previous      # last crashed instance
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl describe pod <pod>          # Events section at bottom
kubectl get pods -o wide            # node, IP, restarts
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh        # poke inside
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<ctr>  # distroless

column1: What do the domain weights add up to on the CKA?
column2: Storage 10%, Workloads & Scheduling 15%, Networking 20%, Troubleshooting 30%, Cluster Architecture 25%. Troubleshooting is the biggest single slice.

column1: What does the ROW-X mnemonic cover for PV access modes?
column2: RWO (ReadWriteOnce), O = ROX (ReadOnlyMany), W = RWX (ReadWriteMany), X = RWOP (ReadWriteOncePod, single pod). Node vs pod scope matters.

column1: What is ReadWriteOnce vs ReadWriteOncePod?
column2: RWO: volume mountable read-write by a single node (many pods on that node OK). RWOP: read-write by a single pod only.

column1: What does RD-R stand for in PV reclaim policies?
column2: Retain (keep data, manual cleanup), Delete (delete backing storage), Recycle (deprecated scrub). Default for dynamic provisioning is usually Delete.

column1: How does a PVC bind to a PV?
column2: By matching storageClassName, access modes, and a capacity request the PV can satisfy. Binding is exclusive and one-to-one.

column1: What is a StorageClass used for?
column2: Defines a provisioner + parameters for dynamic PV provisioning. A PVC referencing it gets a PV created on demand. Mark one default with the storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class annotation.

column1: What volumeBindingMode delays PV binding until a pod is scheduled?
column2: WaitForFirstConsumer (vs Immediate). Useful for topology-aware provisioning so the volume lands in the right zone.

column1: What does SHUR-R mean for Deployment rollout verbs?
column2: Set image, History, Undo (rollback), Restart, Rollout status. The core kubectl rollout / set operations.

column1: How do you roll back a Deployment to the previous revision?
column2: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>. Add --to-revision=N to target a specific one (see with rollout history).

column1: How do you trigger a rolling restart of a Deployment without changing the image?
column2: kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>. Patches a pod-template annotation so pods recycle.

column1: How do you scale a Deployment imperatively?
column2: kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=N. Use --current-replicas=M to make it conditional.

column1: What are the maxSurge and maxUnavailable defaults for a RollingUpdate?
column2: Both default to 25%. maxSurge = extra pods above desired allowed; maxUnavailable = pods that can be down during the update.

column1: What controller runs a pod on every (matching) node?
column2: A DaemonSet. Great for node-level agents (logging, CNI, monitoring). It tolerates control-plane taints if configured.

column1: What is the difference between a Job and a CronJob?
column2: A Job runs pods to successful completion N times. A CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule. Watch concurrencyPolicy and startingDeadlineSeconds.

column1: How do you expose a Deployment as a Service imperatively?
column2: kubectl expose deployment <name> --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=ClusterIP. Also creates the selector from the Deployment labels.

column1: What does NATTS-P summarize for scheduling levers?
column2: NodeSelector, Affinity (node/pod), Taints, Tolerations, Spread (topology spread constraints), Priority/Preemption. The knobs for where pods land.

column1: What is the difference between nodeSelector and node affinity?
column2: nodeSelector is a simple exact label match (hard). Node affinity supports required vs preferred rules and set-based operators (In, NotIn, Exists).

column1: What do the taint effects NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute do (NoS/NoE/NoX)?
column2: NoSchedule: no new pods without matching toleration. PreferNoSchedule: soft avoid. NoExecute: also evicts running pods lacking a toleration.

column1: How do you add a taint to a node?
column2: kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:NoSchedule. Remove it with a trailing dash: kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:NoSchedule-.

column1: What is a topology spread constraint for?
column2: Evenly distributing pods across failure domains (zones, nodes) via topologyKey + maxSkew. Controls balance, not just placement.

column1: How do you cordon, drain, and uncordon a node?
column2:
# 1. stop new pods landing (safe, reversible)
kubectl cordon node1

# 2. evict existing pods for maintenance
kubectl drain node1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
#   --ignore-daemonsets : DaemonSet pods can't be evicted anyway
#   --delete-emptydir-data : required if any pod uses emptyDir
#   --force : also removes bare pods not backed by a controller

# 3. bring it back into rotation
kubectl uncordon node1
Drain respects PodDisruptionBudgets and can block if eviction would violate one.

column1: What does the CNL-E mnemonic cover for Service types?
column2: ClusterIP (internal, default), NodePort (port on every node), LoadBalancer (external LB), ExternalName (CNAME to external DNS). ClusterIP→NodePort→LB build on each other.

column1: What is a ClusterIP Service?
column2: The default type: a stable virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster. Backs Service discovery for pods.

column1: What NodePort range does Kubernetes use by default?
column2: 30000-32767. A NodePort Service opens that port on every node and forwards to the ClusterIP.

column1: What does a Kubernetes Service selector do?
column2: Matches pod labels to build the Endpoints/EndpointSlice list of backends. No selector means you manage Endpoints manually.

column1: What does GC→G→R describe in the Gateway API?
column2: GatewayClass (implementation) → Gateway (listener/infra) → Route (HTTPRoute etc. attaching to the Gateway). The Gateway API layering.

column1: How is Ingress different from a Service?
column2: A Service does L4 (TCP/UDP) load balancing; Ingress does L7 HTTP routing (host/path rules) and needs an Ingress controller to work.

column1: What is the default pod-to-pod network policy behavior?
column2: Allow all until a NetworkPolicy selects a pod; then that pod is default-deny for the selected direction (ingress/egress) except what policies permit.

column1: How do you create a default-deny-all ingress NetworkPolicy?
column2: A NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress], and no ingress rules. It selects all pods and permits nothing inbound.

column1: What CoreDNS Service name resolves inside the cluster for a Service?
column2: <svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Pods get a search domain so <svc> or <svc>.<ns> often resolves too.

column1: Which kubectl command shows why a pod is Pending?
column2: kubectl describe pod <name> and read the Events at the bottom (insufficient CPU/mem, unschedulable, unbound PVC, taints).

column1: What does CJK stand for when the API server is down?
column2:
crictl (inspect containers) → journalctl (service logs) → kubelet (the node agent). The on-node toolkit when kubectl can't reach the API. SSH to the control-plane node, then:
# is the kubelet even up?
sudo systemctl status kubelet
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -f

# inspect the static-pod containers directly via the CRI
sudo crictl ps -a            # find apiserver/etcd containers
sudo crictl logs <container-id>

# the usual culprit: a bad edit in the manifest
sudo less /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
Fix the manifest; the kubelet auto-recreates the static pod within seconds.

column1: Where do static pod manifests live and what watches them?
column2: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, watched by the kubelet. Control-plane components run as static pods created from here.

column1: How do you check kubelet status and logs on a node?
column2: systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet -f. The kubelet is a systemd service, not a pod.

column1: How do you inspect a running container with crictl when kubectl is unavailable?
column2: crictl ps to list, crictl logs <id> for logs, crictl inspect <id> for details. Uses the CRI socket directly.

column1: What does CrashLoopBackOff mean and how do you diagnose it?
column2: The container repeatedly starts and exits; kubelet backs off restarts. Check kubectl logs <pod> --previous and describe for the exit code/reason.

column1: How do you read logs from the previous crashed container instance?
column2: kubectl logs <pod> --previous (or -p). Essential for CrashLoopBackOff where the current container is gone.

column1: What does ImagePullBackOff usually indicate?
column2: Kubelet can't pull the image: wrong name/tag, private registry without imagePullSecret, or registry unreachable. Confirm via describe pod events.

column1: How do you check control-plane component health quickly?
column2: kubectl get pods -n kube-system for static pods, plus kubectl get componentstatuses (deprecated) or hit /healthz / /readyz on the API server.

column1: What does DUCK-U describe for a kubeadm upgrade?
column2:
Drain → Upgrade kubeadm → Control-plane apply → Kubelet+kubectl → Uncordon. One node at a time; control plane before workers.
Control-plane node:
kubectl drain cp1 --ignore-daemonsets
sudo apt-mark unhold kubeadm && sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.34.1-1.1 && sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm
sudo kubeadm upgrade plan
sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34.1
sudo apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl && sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.34.1-1.1 kubectl=1.34.1-1.1 && sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon cp1
Workers are the same but use sudo kubeadm upgrade node instead of apply, and drain/uncordon from a control-plane node.

column1: In a kubeadm upgrade, what is upgraded before the kubelet?
column2: The kubeadm binary, then kubeadm upgrade apply <ver> (control plane) or kubeadm upgrade node (workers). Only then bump kubelet + kubectl and restart kubelet.

column1: What command upgrades the control plane with kubeadm?
column2: kubeadm upgrade plan to preview, then sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.XX.Y on the first control-plane node.

column1: How do you back up etcd with etcdctl?
column2:
Snapshot with API v3, pointing at etcd's endpoint and its PKI certs:
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/snap.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# confirm it's a real snapshot
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/snap.db --write-out=table
Top failure under pressure: forgetting ETCDCTL_API=3 or the three cert flags.

column1: How do you restore an etcd snapshot?
column2:
Restore to a NEW data dir, then repoint etcd's static pod at it:
# 1. restore into a fresh directory
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/snap.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore

# 2. edit the static pod manifest
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
#    - volume hostPath path        -> /var/lib/etcd-restore
#    - --data-dir flag (if present) -> /var/lib/etcd-restore

# 3. kubelet recreates etcd; watch it come back
sudo crictl ps | grep etcd
Gotcha: restore does NOT reuse the live data dir - you must point the manifest at the new one.

column1: Where is the etcd static pod manifest and its data directory?
column2: Manifest: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml. Default data dir: /var/lib/etcd. Certs under /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd.

column1: How do you generate a kubeadm join command for a new node?
column2: kubeadm token create --print-join-command on a control-plane node. Prints the full kubeadm join with token and CA cert hash.

column1: What are the four RBAC objects?
column2: Role and ClusterRole (permissions), RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding (grant them to subjects). Role/RoleBinding are namespaced; ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding are cluster-wide.

column1: What is the difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
column2: A Role grants permissions within a single namespace. A ClusterRole is cluster-scoped and can also cover cluster resources (nodes) and be reused across namespaces via RoleBindings.

column1: How do you test whether a subject can perform an action (RBAC)?
column2: kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource>, optionally --as <user> and -n <ns> to impersonate and scope. Returns yes/no.

column1: How do you create a Role and bind it to a ServiceAccount imperatively?
column2: kubectl create role r --verb=get,list --resource=pods then kubectl create rolebinding rb --role=r --serviceaccount=ns:sa.

column1: What is a ServiceAccount and how do pods use it?
column2: A namespaced identity for pods. Pods reference it via spec.serviceAccountName; a projected token is mounted for API auth. Defaults to the namespace's default SA.

column1: What does Kustomize do and what is its entry file?
column2: Template-free YAML customization via kustomization.yaml: bases, overlays, patches, name prefixes, common labels. Apply with kubectl apply -k <dir>.

column1: How do you preview Kustomize output without applying it?
column2: kubectl kustomize <dir> renders the merged manifests to stdout. Use kubectl apply -k to actually apply.

column1: What is a Helm chart and what command installs one?
column2: A packaged set of templated Kubernetes manifests + values. Install with helm install <release> <chart>; override with --set key=val or -f values.yaml.

column1: How do you see what Helm will render or upgrade a release?
column2: helm template <chart> (render locally) or helm upgrade <release> <chart> to change a running release. helm list shows installed releases.

column1: What is the fastest way to generate a resource YAML skeleton?
column2: Imperative + dry-run: kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx $do > deploy.yaml (with do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"). Edit, then kubectl apply -f.

column1: What is the exam-day non-negotiable before submitting each task?
column2: Verify: re-run get/describe against the correct context and namespace to confirm the change actually took effect. Never assume a command succeeded.

column1: How does an HTTPRoute attach to a Gateway and reach a Service?
column2: Via parentRefs (names the Gateway it binds to) and backendRefs (the target Service(s) + port). backendRefs can be weighted for canary/traffic splitting - something plain Ingress can't do.

column1: What is the role-oriented ownership model of the Gateway API?
column2: Three tiers: GatewayClass (infra provider), Gateway (cluster operator owns listeners/ports), HTTPRoute (app developer owns routing rules). Separation Ingress lacked - it crammed everything into annotations.

column1: Migrating Ingress to Gateway API: what maps to what?
column2: Ingress controller -> GatewayClass + Gateway (listeners). Ingress host/path rules -> HTTPRoute (hostnames, matches, backendRefs). Gateway API is a set of CRDs, so kubectl get gateway,httproute only works once they're installed.

column1: Why might kubectl get gateway return "the server doesn't have a resource type"?
column2: Gateway API is not built in - it's installed as CRDs. If the CRDs aren't applied, the types don't exist yet. Install them (e.g. from the gateway-api release manifests) before creating Gateways/HTTPRoutes.

column1: How long do kubeadm-generated certificates last, and how do you renew them?
column2:
Client certs expire after 1 year. Renew, then restart the control-plane static pods so they load the new certs:
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration     # see what's expiring
sudo kubeadm certs renew all            # regenerate in /etc/kubernetes/pki

# force static pods to reload: move manifests out and back
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests /etc/kubernetes/manifests.bak
sleep 20
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests.bak /etc/kubernetes/manifests

# refresh your admin kubeconfig too if it expired
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
Renewing alone isn't enough - the running apiserver/etcd keep the OLD certs until restarted.

column1: How do you check certificate expiration on a control-plane node?
column2: kubeadm certs check-expiration lists every cert and its expiry. On the exam, an "expired apiserver cert" scenario means kubectl fails while workloads keep running - diagnose offline via the files in /etc/kubernetes/pki.

column1: Do worker node kubelet certificates auto-renew?
column2: Yes - the kubelet supports automatic client cert rotation (it requests a new cert as expiry nears via the CSR API). Control-plane certs from kubeadm do NOT auto-renew; you renew those manually.

column1: What is a CRD and how do you discover a custom resource's fields?
column2: A CustomResourceDefinition extends the API with new resource types. After it's applied, use kubectl explain <kind> and kubectl api-resources to discover the kind, its apiVersion/group, and whether it's Namespaced or Cluster-scoped.

column1: How do you list all resource types and their API groups?
column2: kubectl api-resources (add --namespaced=true/false to filter scope). kubectl api-versions lists group/versions. Essential when a task uses a CRD or a resource you don't know the short name for.

column1: What is an Operator in Kubernetes?
column2: A controller that watches a CRD and reconciles real-world state to match the spec - encoding operational knowledge (backups, upgrades) as code. CRD defines the API; the operator's controller acts on it.

column1: What are the three liveness/readiness/startup probes for?
column2: liveness: restart the container if it's dead. readiness: remove the pod from Service endpoints until ready (no restart). startup: gate the other probes for slow-starting apps. Confusing readiness with liveness is a classic trap.

column1: A pod is Running but gets no traffic. What probe-related cause is likely?
column2: A failing readiness probe: the pod stays out of the Service's Endpoints/EndpointSlice, so it receives no traffic even though it's not restarting. Check kubectl describe pod and endpoints.

column1: What is the difference between resource requests and limits?
column2: requests: what the scheduler reserves (used for placement). limits: the hard ceiling the kubelet enforces (CPU throttled, memory over-limit = OOMKilled). Pending pods often mean requests exceed allocatable.

column1: What causes an OOMKilled container and where do you see it?
column2: The container exceeded its memory limit. kubectl describe pod shows Reason: OOMKilled and the last state/exit code (137). Fix by raising the limit or reducing usage.

column1: What is a PodDisruptionBudget and why does it matter during a drain?
column2: A PDB (minAvailable/maxUnavailable) limits how many pods of an app can be voluntarily disrupted at once. kubectl drain respects it and can block/stall if evicting would violate the budget.

column1: How do you use kubectl debug to troubleshoot a running pod?
column2: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> attaches an ephemeral container sharing the pod's namespaces - handy for distroless images with no shell. kubectl debug node/<node> gives a host-level debug pod.

column1: How do you debug a node itself with kubectl debug?
column2: kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox creates a pod on that node with the host filesystem mounted at /host and host namespaces - lets you inspect the node without SSH.

column1: What does a mirror pod represent?
column2: The kubelet creates a read-only mirror pod in the API server for each static pod so you can see it with kubectl get pods. You can't edit it via the API - you edit the manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests instead.

column1: How do you find which node and why a pod failed to schedule, fast?
column2: kubectl get pod -o wide (node/IP) and kubectl describe pod -> Events. For cluster-wide signal: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp or kubectl events --for pod/<name>.

column1: How do you mount a ConfigMap or Secret as files in a pod?
column2: As a volume: define a configMap/secret volume and a volumeMounts entry. Each key becomes a file. Use subPath to mount a single key without hiding the rest of the target directory.

column1: What does subPath do and what is its gotcha?
column2: subPath mounts a single file/dir from a volume instead of the whole volume, so it doesn't clobber existing files in the mount dir. Gotcha: files mounted via subPath do NOT receive ConfigMap/Secret updates automatically.

column1: What is a headless Service and when do you use it?
column2: A Service with clusterIP: None. No load-balancing VIP; DNS returns the pod IPs directly. Used by StatefulSets so each pod gets a stable DNS name (pod-0.svc...).

column1: How do you write an egress-restricting NetworkPolicy?
column2: Set policyTypes: [Egress] and define egress rules (to ipBlock/namespaceSelector/podSelector + ports). Remember to also allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns) or name resolution breaks.

column1: Common NetworkPolicy trap: what breaks when you lock down egress?
column2:
DNS. A default-deny egress policy blocks lookups to CoreDNS, so apps fail to resolve Service names (connections just hang). Always re-allow port 53 to kube-system:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53

column1: What are CNI, CSI, and CRI?
column2: Extension interfaces: CNI (Container Network Interface - pod networking plugins like Calico/Cilium), CSI (Container Storage Interface - storage drivers), CRI (Container Runtime Interface - containerd/CRI-O). Know which layer a failure is in.

column1: A newly added node stays NotReady with no pod network. Which extension is likely at fault?
column2: The CNI plugin: no CNI installed or its DaemonSet pod isn't running on that node, so the kubelet reports NotReady (network not ready). Check the CNI DaemonSet in kube-system and /etc/cni/net.d.

column1: How do you cross-namespace copy or generate YAML for an unknown resource?
column2:
# generate fresh YAML without touching the cluster
kubectl get <res> <name> -o yaml --dry-run=client > res.yaml

# OR read an existing resource and strip the status
kubectl get <res> <name> -o yaml | grep -vE '^status:|^\s*phase:' | grep -v '^metadata:' | sed '/^metadata:/a\  namespace: new-ns' > res.yaml

# check unknown fields with explain
kubectl explain <res>.spec
kubectl explain <res>.spec.containers
The `--dry-run=client` pattern is safest for editing; it generates the YAML without creating the resource.

column1: What is the fastest way to filter resources server-side?
column2: --field-selector (e.g. kubectl get pods --field-selector status.phase=Running) and -l label selectors. Faster and cleaner than piping through grep, and less error-prone under time pressure.

column1: Use Helm or Kustomize to install a cluster component: which kubectl verbs?
column2: Kustomize is built into kubectl: kubectl apply -k <dir> (preview with kubectl kustomize). Helm is separate: helm install/upgrade/template. The Feb-2025 exam explicitly expects both.

column1: What is the etcdctl gotcha most people miss on restore?
column2: Restore creates a NEW data dir; you must repoint etcd to it. Also set ETCDCTL_API=3 and pass --cacert/--cert/--key - forgetting the API version or certs is the top reason the command fails under exam pressure.
